articles.title: The Definition for a Heart Attack Just Changed—and It Could Help Women in a Big Way
articles.summary: Cardiologists around the world just changed the definition of a heart attack. Here's why it may help women.
articles.body:
Most people are aware of the general mechanism behind a heart attack : Blood flow to the heart is reduced or blocked, causing damage to the organ. But the exact medical definition is actually a lot more complicated; it classifies heart attacks into different categories, each with its own urgency and treatment plan.

Now, four major cardiology associations around the world have agreed on a new definition for heart attack—and it could help more women get diagnosed so they can get the timely treatment they need.

Meet the experts: Ravi Shah, M.D ., associate director of the cardiac care unit at Northwell's Lenox Hill Hospital; Sanjiv Patel, M.D ., interventional cardiologist at MemorialCare Heart & Vascular Institute at Orange Coast Medical Center in Fountain Valley, CA

The new definition comes courtesy of the European Society of Cardiology (ESC), the American College of Cardiology (ACC), the American Heart Association (AHA), and the World Heart Federation (WHF). It's a "simplified" classification system that breaks heart attacks, a.k.a. myocardial infarction, into three categories and changes priorities and diagnostic criteria for them. That includes increasing emphasis on some less common forms of heart attack, which commonly affect women more than men, according to Sanjiv Patel, M.D ., interventional cardiologist at MemorialCare Heart & Vascular Institute at Orange Coast Medical Center in Fountain Valley, CA.

This updated definition of a heart attack follows the 2025 " Great Debate " in the European Heart Journal that spotlighted the vagueness of the previous definition and the complicated medical jargon that made it tough to make shared decisions with patients, says Ravi Shah, M.D ., associate director of the cardiac care unit at Northwell's Lenox Hill Hospital. "I would have some patients say, 'I had a stage four heart attack, so it wasn't a 'bad' heart attack?'" Dr. Patel says. "It's confusing for patients."

To be clear, any heart attack is still a heart attack—and all heart attacks are serious. But the new definition reclassifies types of heart attacks and creates a simpler understanding for everyone involved. Here's how it works, plus why doctors say it's a good thing for women.

What's the new definition of a heart attack?

The new guidelines break heart attacks into three categories:

Primary : This happens suddenly and is caused by severe reduction or a blockage of blood flow to the heart.

Secondary : This occurs due to an imbalance in oxygen supply and demand in the heart due to another acute condition.

Procedure-related : These happen as a complication from surgery.

The new definition also changes the threshold for women to be diagnosed with a heart attack based on a level of a protein called troponin in their blood, which is released when the heart is injured. "Baseline normal levels of troponin are lower in females than males," Dr. Patel says. But previous definitions had a universal baseline for both sexes.

As a result, women having a heart attack were at a greater risk of being misdiagnosed than men when doctors looked at troponin, he explains. The new changes provide a lower limit for women, which can catch heart attacks that the previous levels may have missed.

Why are these changes helpful for women?

There are a few reasons why these changes can benefit women. The new definition emphasizes identifying the underlying cause of a heart attack , Dr. Shah says. Take spontaneous coronary artery dissection (SCAD), which occurs when a tear in the heart's artery blocks blood flow to the heart. Women make up about 90% of its cases, and it's often under-recognized and misdiagnosed, he says. The previous definition put SCAD into an "ambiguous" category, Dr. Shah points out. "This new framework moves SCAD into the primary myocardial infarction definition and will hopefully help increase prompt recognition and diagnosis," he says.

The sex-specific troponin thresholds can also help detect a heart attack in women sooner, Dr. Shah says. Not only that, the new definition encourages the use of imaging to define the cause of heart attack. "Both will help address the current disparities in the diagnosis and treatment of heart attacks in women," he adds.

Women are more likely to have signs of a heart attack that are considered "atypical" compared to men, who more often present with the classic chest pain and pressure. This makes it more important to dive deeper when they're not well, Dr. Patel says. "They might have sharp pain, nausea , or shortness of breath compared to the traditional symptoms you expect," he says. "Sometimes people might not consider those symptoms as someone is having a heart attack, and they might not get properly treated." The new definition doesn't necessarily change awareness for patients of these symptoms, but it does provide more tools for doctors to detect heart attacks in people who may not have classic signs.

What to do if you suspect you're having a heart attack

While the definition for diagnosis has gotten fine-tuned, the guidance around what to do if you are having a heart attack hasn't changed. "In cardiology, we say 'time is muscle'—prompt diagnosis and treatment of a heart attack is crucial," says Dr. Shah.

If you suspect you're having a heart attack, he recommends getting to the emergency room ASAP. Dr. Patel suggests being evaluated if you're unsure if you're having a heart attack, too. "Because of the atypical nature of symptoms in females, they tend to brush it off as 'just' stomach pain or something else," he says. "But when they realize something is wrong 1.5 hours later, they're already 1.5 hours into a potential heart attack, which is not a great thing. Time matters."

While it may be inconvenient to take a trip to the ER, Dr. Patel says it's important to get checked out. "If it's not a heart attack, it's not—great," he says. "But if it is, it's a big deal. You can save your life, and save yourself a lifetime of medical problems if you get diagnosed and treated quickly."

articles.title: These 8 foods and drinks may be hurting your sleep — here’s what experts say to avoid
articles.summary: Caffeine can linger for hours, while other nighttime favorites may take longer to digest, trigger reflux or otherwise interfere with restful sleep.
articles.body:
Our experts independently review everything we recommend. If you buy through our links, we may earn commission.

Trouble falling asleep ? Feeling like acid is creeping back up your throat? Your dinner or bedtime snack might be to blame. But going to bed with your stomach rumbling isn't exactly ideal either. The good news is that you don't have to avoid eating or drinking before bedtime entirely. The key is being strategic.

"Ideally, you should eat your last big meal of the day at least two to three hours before lying down for bed. This can help you reduce the chance of nighttime reflux, make you more comfortable and promote a good night's sleep," says gastroenterologist Dr. Edmundo Rodriguez-Frias . But that doesn't mean you need to stop eating altogether. "It's important to honor your body's hunger cues. If you are hungry before bed, I would recommend eating a small, light snack to tide you over until breakfast," he adds.

Timing isn't the only thing that matters — what you eat or drink is just as important. To help you decode the habits that may be making it hard to sleep comfortably at night, and what to eat or drink instead, I used my expertise as a dietitian to dig into the latest research and guidelines and consulted four health experts, including two doctors, a fellow dietitian and a neuroscientist who specializes in sleep. Here are the eight foods and drinks they recommend avoiding before bed and what to reach for instead.

✅ What to do instead: Cut caffeine after lunch (or six to eight hours before bed) and reach for a caffeine-free swap, like chamomile or rooibos tea.

It may be tempting to grab a pick-me-up during the 3 p.m. slump, but doing so could work against you later. "Caffeine is a stimulant that can make it harder to fall asleep and reduce total sleep time, even when consumed several hours before bed," says Dr. Fariha Abbasi-Feinberg , a sleep specialist and spokesperson for the American Academy of Sleep Medicine.

According to a 2023 review , the half-life of caffeine varies widely among individuals, ranging from two to 10 hours. To avoid reductions in total sleep time, researchers estimated that a standard cup of coffee should be consumed at least 8.8 hours before bedtime. Caffeine isn't limited to your morning latte: soda, energy drinks , green and black tea and some protein bars and powders can be hidden sources.

We've tested the best teas for sleep , and if you want something cozy to wind down with in the evening, we recommend the caffeine-free Numi and Tazo options featured below. Rooibos tea is another caffeine-free alternative.

✅ What to do instead: Mix up a mocktail or try a nonalcoholic beverage.

Alcohol may make you feel drowsy at first, but Abbasi-Feinberg warns that it can disrupt sleep later in the night, leading to poorer-quality rest overall .

Chelsie Rohrscheib , PhD, head sleep expert and neuroscientist at Wesper, agrees. "Alcohol is initially sedating and may help you fall asleep," she explains. "But as the alcohol is metabolized in the liver, it's converted into a byproduct that's actually stimulating and wake-promoting to the brain. This can lead to sleep fragmentation and insomnia in the second half of the night."

If you're craving something to help you unwind, look for beverages or supplements formulated to promote relaxation without alcohol. Magnesium glycinate is a popular option that may support rest, and it's often paired with L-theanine — a calming amino acid — in sleep and stress-relief formulas. Chamomile and lemon balm are also common in sleep teas for their stress-relieving properties.

If you're after something more festive, the non-alcoholic (NA) market has expanded well beyond sparkling apple cider — you'll find NA beer, wine and even alcohol-free whiskey and tequila. Just note that some NA drinks are carbonated, which may worsen reflux in people who are sensitive to it. If you are making a mocktail, consider using tart cherry juice. Tart cherries contain natural melatonin and tryptophan, meaning they may help you fall asleep more easily.

✅ What to do instead: Prioritize low-sugar snacks that contain fiber or protein.

"Sugary foods and simple carbohydrates cause an initial spike in blood sugar, followed by a quick crash," says Rohrscheib, which can make it harder to stay asleep. "When your brain detects that your blood glucose levels are low, it will wake you up to eat, since starvation is considered more of a survival threat than sleep loss."

So instead of reaching for a cookie or a pint of ice cream, opt for something that's easy to digest and includes protein or fiber. Protein bars can work well, depending on the ingredients, as can cottage cheese and Greek yogurt. Almonds are another solid choice — beyond healthy fats and protein, they're rich in magnesium , a mineral that may support sleep and relaxation. If cereal is your go-to nighttime snack, swap in a lower-sugar option with some protein or fiber to help keep blood sugar levels stable.

Catalina Crunch Protein Cereal, Blueberry Muffin

✅ What to do instead: Swap peppermint tea and candies for ginger tea and chews.

Peppermint is often used after meals to settle the stomach, but registered dietitian Jana Hand notes that it can actually work against you: Because peppermint may relax the lower esophageal sphincter, it can make reflux more likely instead of easing it.

If you want something to soothe an unsettled stomach, ginger is a solid alternative. You'll find ginger tea at most grocery stores, along with ginger chews — just look for options that are low in added sugar.

✅ What to do instead: Opt for vanilla- or fruit-flavored treats instead.

This one might be the hardest to hear: Both Hand and Rodriguez-Frias included chocolate on their lists because it may relax the lower esophageal sphincter, making reflux more likely.

It's also often high in added sugar and, as Abbasi-Feinberg points out, does contain some caffeine, even if the amount is small.

Instead, swap in a non-chocolate treat that's lower in added sugar. Flavored almonds are a great option, since almonds also provide magnesium. If you're craving something cold, try frozen yogurt bars, like Yasso.

SkinnyDipped Lemon Bliss Almonds, 24-pack

Yasso Sea Salt Caramel Frozen Greek Yogurt Bar

✅ What to do instead: Opt for baked or air-fried versions, and watch your portion sizes.

Fat takes longer to digest than simple carbs, which is usually a plus for staying full — but at night, that becomes a drawback. Because your body is still working to break down fat, high-fat foods can make it harder to fall asleep and may trigger reflux, especially if they're fried or greasy.

"Gravity is very important for preventing acid reflux throughout the night during the breakdown of food in the stomach," explains Rodriguez-Frias. "If you lie down directly after a meal, gravity is no longer able to keep your stomach contents inside your stomach where it belongs, and stomach acid can begin to creep up your esophagus, causing that classic heartburn pain."

So instead of ordering mozzarella sticks or a bacon-topped burger, look for ways to cut back on fat, and opt for healthier fats — like avocado or olive oil — when you can. Air fryers are a great way to get a similar crispy texture without all the added fat from deep-frying, and baking or roasting works just as well if you'd rather skip another appliance.

✅ What to do instead: Use mild seasoning blends, and save spicy dishes for lunch or early dinner.

Hand recommends avoiding spicy foods before bed, especially if you regularly experience reflux. Rohrscheib agrees: "When we lie down, the contents of our stomach are more likely to flow back into the esophagus, causing pain and discomfort. Spicy, acidic and fatty foods are more likely to cause this discomfort, leading to indigestion and heartburn during sleep."

The fix is simple, if a little disappointing for spice lovers: save the hot sauce, spicy curries and hot chips for lunch or an early dinner. If you're eating closer to bedtime, reach for a milder seasoning blend instead.

McCormick Salt Free Garlic and Herb Seasoning

✅ What to do instead: Choose lower-acid fruits and vegetables.

Acidic foods can also aggravate reflux, which is why Hand puts tomatoes, oranges, grapefruits, pineapple and salsa on the avoid-before-bed list.

Instead, she recommends reaching for lower-acid fruit — bananas are a favorite among several experts as a solid bedtime snack.

If cutting out acidic foods entirely isn't realistic, staying upright for a while after eating can help rather than lying flat right away. Skip the stack of pillows , which can strain your neck, and try a wedge pillow instead. It's also worth asking your doctor about alginate-based supplements if you have gastroesophageal reflux disease and experience regular breakthrough reflux.

Edmundo Rodriguez-Frias , MD, board-certified physician specializing in gastroenterology and geriatric medicine and medical contributor at Full of Life recovery center

Jana Hand , registered dietitian and founder at Helping Hand Nutrition

Chelsie Rohrscheib , PhD, head sleep researcher and neuroscientist at Wesper

A note on supplements: The products included on this list are dietary supplements. Statements about these products have not been evaluated by the Food and Drug Administration . These products are not intended to diagnose, treat, cure, or prevent any disease. Dietary supplements are not appropriate for everyone and may interact with other supplements or medications, so talk to your health care provider before adding one to your routine.

articles.title: Common cholesterol drug linked to lower dementia risk when started early
articles.summary: A massive study found that starting statins within a year of a type 2 diabetes diagnosis was linked to a 15% lower risk of dementia over a decade.
articles.body: Starting statin therapy shortly after a type 2 diabetes diagnosis may not only protect the heart — it may also be linked to a lower dementia risk. A large study presented at the European Society of Cardiology Congress in Munich on Aug. 30 found that adults who began taking a statin within one year of their type 2 diabetes diagnosis had a 15% lower relative risk of developing dementia over 10 years compared to those who did not take the medication within five years. Even for those who delayed starting a statin for one to five years, there was still a 10% lower relative risk, according to the findings, which were published in The Lancet Regional Health – Europe. 3 THINGS TO AVOID IN MIDDLE AGE COULD MEAN 13 MORE YEARS WITHOUT DEMENTIA, STUDY FINDS A statin is a prescription medication that lowers "bad" LDL cholesterol and helps reduce the risk of heart attack and stroke. Researchers conducted the study by tracking health data from 132,585 patients in Denmark who were diagnosed with type 2 diabetes between 2006 and 2019 and had no prior history of statin use or dementia. During a median follow-up of 7.1 years, the team analyzed how the timing of statin treatment impacted overall dementia rates. Dr. Liron Sinvani, a geriatrician and director for research and innovation at the Northwell Institute for Healthy Aging in New York, said this was a "well-designed, large-scale observational study that adds to a growing body of evidence suggesting that statins may help protect brain health." GAME-CHANGING CHOLESTEROL PILL WINS FDA APPROVAL AFTER CUTTING LDL NEARLY 60% She noted that while a 15% reduction is a modest improvement, it remains "very significant." People with type 2 diabetes have an increased risk of cognitive decline and heart disease, consistent with previous research. Although guidelines generally recommend statins for many adults ages 40 to 75 with diabetes, statin treatment is not always started soon after a type 2 diabetes diagnosis. The study also examined whether the timing of treatment was linked to dementia risk. People who started statins within a year of their diagnosis had a lower risk than those who did not begin treatment. CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES "The message here is that maybe waiting is actually not the right approach," Sinvani said, supporting earlier consideration of statin therapy in routine diabetes care. The expert said she found the results "especially compelling" because the benefit was driven by a lower risk of vascular dementia rather than Alzheimer's disease. "The message here is that maybe waiting is actually not the right approach." "And that makes biological sense, because we know statins lower cholesterol, reduces inflammation and protects blood vessels," she added, pointing out that these same mechanisms prevent vascular damage to the brain. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER Statin therapy should be viewed as one piece of a broader health strategy alongside exercising regularly, adhering to a healthy diet and staying socially connected, according to the expert. Almost half of dementia cases may be preventable or delayable by addressing modifiable risk factors, according to the Lancet Commission. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ The study did have limitations. Because it was observational rather than a randomized clinical trial, the researchers could not definitively state that statins directly prevent dementia. As Sinvani cautioned, "This is not proof that statins prevent dementia, but I think it's an important step in this literature." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The doctor encouraged people with type 2 diabetes who are not taking a statin to ask their doctor whether the medication is appropriate for them."

articles.title: Nepal rescuers try to reach dozens trapped in tunnel after two pulled out alive
articles.summary: More than 1,300 people have died and thousands are missing, but rescuers' hopes have risen after finding survivors in a tunnel.
articles.body:
Rescuers in Nepal are stepping up efforts to find scores of workers believed to be trapped in tunnels, nine days after the devastating flash floods which hit the area on the border with Tibet in China.

Hopes have risen after two people were pulled out alive on Friday. The body of a third person was also found in one of the tunnels used to supply hydropower stations.

The massive flash flood, believed to have been triggered by a glacial collapse, swept through a Himalayan valley last Wednesday, wiping out entire villages.

There are now 1,311 confirmed dead and 5,330 still missing in Nepal and Tibet. Hundreds of foreign citizens are believed to be among those missing, from at least 34 countries.

The full impact of the flood in Tibet is unclear. China has released information through state media outlets showing the devastation around the border, but has given few details about the victims or the impact on local villagers.

In Nepal, however, rescue operations are taking place at seven hydropower tunnels in which more than 150 people are feared trapped - as well as in 19 other areas.

In the early hours of Friday morning, rescuers heard what they thought could be voices at the Trishuli 3A hydropower site.

According to local reports, they called out "don't worry, we're here to rescue you" - and heard back a faint "okay".

Crews clambered in to find Sanjaya Shah and Kabir Maharjan - both had injuries on their hands and legs, "possibly" from crawling through the tunnel. Both were airlifted to the Army Hospital in the capital, Kathmandu.

Maharjan, who was rescued second, is in a critical condition, the prime minister's office said. Shah was also undergoing medical tests.

The body of a third person was found in the same tunnel later. A local official said it was swollen and could not be immediately identified.

Officials believe another 39 people are in the Trishuli 3A tunnel, although it is not clear if all are alive.

Col Jhabindra Reshmi said that his teams had rescued more than 400 Nepali nationals and 270 foreign citizens following the flash flooding on 26 August.

He has said mud and rocks have made entering tunnels difficult and rescuers were having to dig access holes to get underground.

Engineers have been pumping air into the tunnels.

Last week's floodwaters washed away a lot of heavy machinery, making it harder for rescuers to unblock tunnels, says a representative for Nepalese power companies.

Uttam Bhlon Lama, vice president at Independent Power Producers of Nepal, told the BBC's Newsday programme that the rescue of the two men on Friday would "motivate the rescuers to do more".

"The flood level is still very high," Lama added.

Nepalese authorities have warned that rainfall may cause additional flooding in the region.

At least 1,287 people are known to have died in Nepal, with 5,083 still missing.

On the Tibetan side, the death toll reported by Chinese media on Friday was 31, with 531 people unaccounted for.

Emergency teams in Tibet appear to be focusing on helping the living rather than holding out hope for more survivors.

Scientists are still studying the exact cause, but it is believed to have been caused by a glacial collapse and climate change may have been a factor.

Moments after the seismic event, which was initially thought to have been an earthquake, a massive wall of water and debris crashed downstream, taking buildings, roads and vehicles with it.

Experts from the Asian Mountain Academic Alliance, the Stimson Centre and China's Institute of Mountain Hazards and Environment said there was evidence of growing instability around the glacier in the days before the collapse and better early-warning systems could have saved lives.

articles.title: Scientists discover new tick-borne virus after testing thousands of patients with mysterious illnesses
articles.summary: The Asian longhorned tick nairovirus caused flu-like illness and thrombocytopenia in over 10% of tick-bitten patients studied in a China lab.
articles.body: Scientists in China have identified a previously unknown tick-borne virus that can cause flu-like illness, fatigue and gastrointestinal symptoms, according to a new study. The newly discovered virus, the Asian longhorned tick nairovirus (ALTNV), which is part of the orthonairovirus group, has also been found to cause thrombocytopenia (reduced blood platelet counts) and laboratory evidence of liver-cell injury or inflammation. Since 2009, Chinese researchers have been tracking patients with unusual illnesses, including severe fever with thrombocytopenia syndrome (SFTS), according to Dr. Sharon Nachman, chief of pediatric infectious diseases at Stony Brook Children’s Hospital in New York. NO CURE, NO VACCINE: EXPERTS WARN OF RARE BOURBON VIRUS AFTER FIRST NY CASE "Thrombocytopenia is low platelet count, so those patients bled, and it had about a 30% mortality, which is quite high," she told Fox News Digital. "So, they kept following those patients." Many of the cases were linked to Dabie bandavirus (DBV), a tick-borne hemorrhagic fever, but it was not the most common virus. After extensive testing of blood samples and viral fragments, researchers identified the new virus, ALTNV, which is genetically distinct from DBV. Researchers from the State Key Laboratory of Pathogen and Biosecurity in Beijing identified the virus in 10.4% of 3,163 patients who had been bitten by ticks. HANTAVIRUS IN THE US: WHERE THE RARE, SOMETIMES DEADLY DISEASE HAS BEEN FOUND Patients who had both ALTNV and DBV were more likely to have respiratory issues and kidney complications. Seven (18.4%) of these patients died during the course of the study. "The cocirculation of ALTNV and DBV in the same areas, coupled with their shared tick vector, underscores the need for improved differential diagnosis between infections with these viruses in regions where SFTS is endemic," the authors concluded. The findings were published this week in the New England Journal of Medicine. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "The big picture is that ticks carry lots of viruses," Nachman said. "We're getting smarter at identifying those viruses. And when one blood sample is negative, it's important to say, 'Maybe there was a new virus there, and let's look for it.'" Symptoms and treatment Illness from ALTNV can initially resemble the flu, causing fever, muscle aches, fatigue and sometimes respiratory symptoms. Although an ALTNV infection can cause low platelet counts, the study did not link the virus alone to severe bleeding or deaths. The fatal cases involved patients who were also infected with DBV, which causes severe fever with thrombocytopenia syndrome. Because tick-borne viral symptoms can overlap with many infections, Nachman emphasized the importance of identifying the specific virus. "Effective antivirals exist for flu, but not for many tick-borne viruses, including the newly identified one," she said. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER For most patients, supportive care is given to help manage symptoms, "but it's also about being smart and not giving patients the wrong medication," Nachman noted. "And we certainly don't want to use antibiotics because those only work for bacteria, not for viruses." Preventing tick bites Nachman shared the best practices she recommends to families looking to avoid tick bites. "Wear the right clothing, meaning long pants, tucking them into your socks, and use tick repellents on your skin if you're an adult or on your clothing if you're a young child," she advised. CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES It’s also important to be on the lookout for ticks on the skin. "The longer the tick is on your skin, the more it's engorged, the more it’s likely to pass an infection to you," Nachman said. "So, removing them after you've gone hiking or walking on the beach will be really important." While the Asian longhorn tick is not yet seen in the U.S., Nachman noted there are "lots and lots of other ticks, and those ticks carry other diseases." "I don't want to say one tick is worse than another tick. It's rather all about the diseases they carry and who you are," she said. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ "So, if you're a healthy adult, and you get babesiosis, you often get better without any medications. But if you're an immune-compromised adult, you're going to be quite sick. "It’s not really about the ticks. It’s about the patient. Who are you? What's your underlying illness if you have any? How old are you, and how healthy are you?"

articles.title: Texas AG Paxton investigates military healthcare contractor over denied claims
articles.summary: Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton has opened an investigation into a major military healthcare contractor over wrongfully denied medical claims.
articles.body: Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton has opened an investigation into a major military healthcare contractor over wrongfully denied medical claims. Paxton’s office said in a release this week that complaints have surged against TriWest Healthcare Alliance because the company is denying claims due to errors that incorrectly listed some beneficiaries as having “Other Health Insurance,” or OHI. “Health insurance companies cannot promise health care coverage and then wrongfully deny patients the benefits they are entitled to receive,” Paxton said in the release. The investigation will examine whether TriWest’s handling of the claims violated Texas consumer protection law. TriWest is one of the contractors that administers TRICARE, the military’s healthcare program for active-duty service members, retirees and their families. In May, NBC News reported on persistent problems beneficiaries have faced since 2025, when TRICARE transitioned its contract from Health Net Federal Services to TriWest. The reporting included the case of Guy Shoemaker, 65, of Fort Worth Texas, who said he had tens of thousands of dollars in previously approved claims overturned and money clawed back from paid providers because of an OHI error. Shoemaker, a retired Army sergeant first class and recruiter who spent a year in Afghanistan, was diagnosed with Stage 2 throat cancer in 2021 and has since needed ongoing therapy to ensure he can speak and swallow safely. The lull in coverage led to serious deterioration of his condition. Another 13 beneficiaries also spoke to NBC News, describing problems with their TRICARE coverage following the transition to TriWest. Paxton, who is currently running for Senate as a Republican against Democrat James Talarico, mentioned Shoemaker in his press release. “Mr. Shoemaker tried to correct the issue with TriWest for almost two years. He only received relief after NBC aired a news story covering his situation,” the press release said. “The Shoemakers’ situation is not unique and TriWest has acknowledged the OHI denials are [a] problem.” Shortly after NBC News’ story on Shoemaker aired, TriWest President and CEO David McIntyre Jr. apologized to those who had experienced problems with OHI errors under the company’s watch. “I want to personally take this opportunity to apologize to those of you who have experienced challenges with Other Health Insurance on our watch,” McIntyre wrote in a letter to beneficiaries in May. In an emailed statement Friday, TriWest said the company is reviewing Paxton’s investigative demand. “We and the 146,000 providers in our Texas network are committed to military families, helping ensure they receive the care they have earned,” the statement said. In an interview Friday, Shoemaker, who is now covered by Medicare, said the Texas investigation is “nice to see,” but believes the issue should be addressed nationally. For him, however, “the damage is done” — even though his coverage problems were resolved, his condition is “going to progressively get worse,” Shoemaker said. “I know the issue still exists for other veterans,” Shoemaker said. “I’ll give Ken Paxton credit. I appreciate the fact that he’s taking it up, but again, it should be more than just state level.” Paxton’s office said it had issued civil investigative demands to TriWest seeking information from the company and plans to interview consumers and employees. The investigation will determine whether TriWest violated the Texas Deceptive Trade Practices Act.

articles.title: Measles cases top 3,000, CDC reports, the highest in more than 3 decades
articles.summary: A 6-week-old baby girl is one of two people with measles who died in Pennsylvania, the Lancaster County coroner said Friday, as the nation’s measles tally hit a new 35-year record of 3,134 cases.
articles.body: A 6-week-old baby girl is one of two people with measles who died in Pennsylvania, the Lancaster County coroner said Friday, as the nation’s measles tally hit a new 35-year record of 3,134 cases. Dr. Stephen Diamantoni told NBC affiliate WGAL that the baby died in August and also had a rare genetic disorder called Amish lethal microcephaly. It’s the second measles-related death in an infant in Lancaster County. A baby boy died shortly after birth in mid-August after his infected mother went into labor a month early. At least 115 more people in Pennsylvania, mostly in Lancaster County, have been diagnosed with measles in the last week, the health department said Friday, bringing the state’s outbreak to about 577 cases within the last few months. Based on new data from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, measles in the U.S. is still accelerating. Outbreaks in Wisconsin and Ohio are picking up speed. Wisconsin has 144 cases, up from 26 a month ago. And 129 cases are now in Ohio, up from just over 60 in the same time period. The number of people across the country who have gotten sick with measles is undoubtedly much higher because many don’t get tested, experts say. The new milestone, the highest number of confirmed cases since 1991, is yet another indication that the highly contagious virus is taking over, particularly in areas of the country with plummeting vaccination rates. Outbreaks are driving up healthcare costs and have led to hundreds of hospitalizations, including of children and pregnant women. “Measles is acting like it’s endemic now. There’s a lot of domestic transmission,” said Dr. Demetre Daskalakis, who directed the CDC’s National Center for Immunization and Respiratory Diseases before resigning last year. “If I were a betting person, I would expect 5,000-plus cases this year.” The ongoing outbreaks are threatening the country’s status of having eliminated measles in 2000. Nearly everyone who’s had measles caught the virus from a family member, a neighbor or another person within U.S. borders, experts say. Just 16 cases were reported among people visiting from other countries. Global health officials are eyeing the U.S. measles situation carefully. In November, a group within the World Health Organization, the Pan American Health Organization (PAHO), will meet to decide whether the U.S. has lost its measles elimination status. PAHO is looking specifically at whether a single chain of measles transmission has gone on for more than 12 months, as well as whether there are a significant number of cases for which the source of infection is unknown, said Noel Brewer, the chair of an independent committee that assists the CDC in analyzing the country’s measles situation ahead of the PAHO meeting. “The country’s had measles cases every week for the last 20 months, and at least one regional outbreak has already passed the 12-month mark,” said Brewer, also a professor of public health at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill. “There’s no end in sight.” Daskalakis likened losing measles elimination status to finding uncontrolled blood pressure during a routine medical checkup: It’s a warning signal of health problems to come. “Measles elimination is more than continuous transmission. It’s also, ‘Do you have a public health system that’s able to respond nimbly? Do you have adequate surveillance? Do you have an environment that’s conducive to high coverage for measles vaccine?’” Daskalakis said. The development would indicate “a loss of faith” in the country’s ability to control outbreaks, said Dr. William Moss, a professor in the departments of epidemiology and international health at the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health. “Getting it back would take a tremendous amount of work,” Moss said. “We would have to stop measles virus transmission in the country, and then undergo a reverification process.” In addition to the Pennsylvania deaths, three others died of complications related to measles in 2025. Those deaths occurred in Texas and New Mexico and were immediately recognized by the CDC. After a public tug-of-war between Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro, who announced the recent deaths during a briefing last week, and Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., who suggested on social media that the deaths had been “fabricated” by one of the governor’s staff members, the CDC hasn’t officially acknowledged the 2026 deaths. On Friday, the CDC referred a request for comment to a post on X from Kennedy saying that the agency “will continue to update its reporting as additional information becomes available.”
